newsitem.title: ECUADOR: Ecuador says telecom sale to go ahead after all.
newsitem.headline: Ecuador says telecom sale to go ahead after all.

text.p: Ecuador said Monday it would go ahead with the sale of one-third of its telephone company Emetel in late April despite and earlier announcement that it would be postponed.

"The privatisation of Emetel is a reference point for everything going on in the country ... By late April the envelopes of the five bidders will be opened," said Rodrigo Paz, chairman of the National Council on Modernisation.
The sale of a 35 percent stake in Emetel was slated for April by the government of former President Abadala Bucaram.
But after Bucaram was declared "mentally incompetent" and removed from office, both the new government and Congress said the sale would be subject to review and probably postponed.
But Paz told foreign correspondents the deal would go through as planned because the country needed to recover the confidence of the world's financial community.

"We must go ahead with this process and make it pristine so as to recover the confidence of the international organizations. For us it is of the outmost importance that it is ready by the end of April," Paz said.
He added World Bank experts would fly to Ecuador in the next few days to help with the sale process.
Emetel will be split in two operational units and bidders will only be allowed to buy into one or the other, but not the two at the same time.

The state will keep a 55 percent share and the remaining 10 percent will be sold to Emetel's employees. But Paz said that after the results of the April tender were analyzed, the government would consider selling an extra chunk of its stake.
U.S. firms MCI and GTE, Italy's Stet, Spain's Telefonica and Korea Telecom all signed up for the Emetel partial privatisation last November.
The government hopes to raise $1.0 billion from the sale of a stake in Emetel, which is valued at $4.0 billion.
Only seven out of 100 inhabitants have a telephone in Ecuador, giving it one of the fewest lines per capita in Latin America.
